summary: Zidovudine (AZT) is the first approved nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, a thymidine analogue used in combination with other antiretrovirals to treat HIV-1 infection and, importantly, to prevent mother-to-child transmission. It is phosphorylated intracellularly to a triphosphate that terminates viral DNA chain elongation. It carries a boxed warning for hematologic toxicity (severe anemia and neutropenia), symptomatic myopathy with prolonged use, and lactic acidosis/severe hepatomegaly with steatosis common to the NRTI class.
indications: Treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination with other antiretroviral agents
Prevention of maternal-fetal (perinatal) HIV-1 transmission - antepartum, intrapartum, and neonatal dosing

Approximately 240 mg/m2 twice daily (per weight bands); max 300 mg/dose

IV 2 mg/kg over 1 hour then 1 mg/kg/hour until cord clamping
Oral 2 mg/kg every 6 hours (or per current weight-based guideline) starting within 6-12 h of birth for 6 weeks

Adjust for accumulation of glucuronide metabolite

Always use in combination with other antiretroviral drugs (never monotherapy for treatment)
Use the IV formulation for intrapartum prophylaxis and when oral therapy is not feasible
Reduce dose in severe renal impairment and in significant hepatic impairment
Monitor blood counts and consider erythropoietin or dose interruption for marrow toxicity
moa: Zidovudine is a thymidine nucleoside analogue that is phosphorylated by cellular kinases to zidovudine triphosphate. This active metabolite competitively inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and is incorporated into the growing viral DNA chain, causing chain termination because it lacks a 3'-hydroxyl group. The result is inhibition of HIV replication.

absolute: Previous potentially life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction to zidovudine (e.g. anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
Abnormally low neutrophil counts or hemoglobin (relative to severity - avoid until corrected)
relative: Pre-existing bone marrow compromise (baseline anemia or neutropenia)
Hepatic impairment or risk factors for hepatic steatosis/lactic acidosis
monitor: Concomitant ganciclovir, interferon, or other marrow-suppressive agents
Patients with obesity or prolonged NRTI exposure (steatosis/lactic acidosis)

preg: Zidovudine is a cornerstone of preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission and is used antepartum, intrapartum (IV) and in the newborn. The Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry has not shown an increased overall risk of birth defects. Benefits in reducing perinatal transmission generally outweigh risks; manage as part of guideline-based combination therapy.
lact: Mothers with HIV should not breastfeed because of the risk of postnatal HIV transmission; zidovudine is also excreted in human milk. In settings where breastfeeding is unavoidable, follow national HIV guidelines.
renal: Zidovudine and its inactive glucuronide metabolite are renally eliminated; reduce the dose in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 15 mL/min) or on hemodialysis (e.g. 100 mg every 6-8 hours). Hemodialysis has negligible effect on zidovudine but enhances removal of the GZDV metabolite.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; reduced metabolism may increase exposure and a dose reduction may be needed. Zidovudine carries class risk of lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis - discontinue if these develop.

major: Stavudine - pharmacologic antagonism; do not co-administer
Ribavirin - antagonism and exacerbation of anemia; avoid combination
Ganciclovir / valganciclovir, interferon alfa and other myelosuppressive agents - additive hematologic toxicity
moderate: Other bone-marrow-suppressive or cytotoxic drugs (e.g. co-trimoxazole, pyrimethamine, dapsone) - increased hematologic toxicity
Probenecid, fluconazole, valproic acid, methadone - increase zidovudine levels by reducing glucuronidation
minor: Phenytoin - variable changes in phenytoin levels; monitor
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; high-fat meals can modestly reduce absorption but no dose change needed.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol due to additive hepatotoxicity and lactic acidosis risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Causes macrocytosis (elevated MCV), anemia and neutropenia; monitor CBC. May raise lactate and liver enzymes.

serious: Severe anemia requiring transfusion and neutropenia (boxed warning)
Symptomatic myopathy with prolonged use (boxed warning)
Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis (boxed warning)
emergency: Lactic acidosis (deep breathing, abdominal pain, weakness)
Severe symptomatic anemia or febrile neutropenia/sepsis

monitoring: Complete blood count (hemoglobin and neutrophils) frequently, especially in advanced HIV disease
Liver function tests; serum lactate if signs of lactic acidosis
Creatine phosphokinase and muscle symptoms (myopathy) with prolonged use
HIV viral load and CD4 count to assess response; signs of immune reconstitution syndrome
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed and always with your other HIV medicines - never alone
Report unusual tiredness, pallor, shortness of breath, fever or sore throat (low blood counts)
Seek urgent care for rapid deep breathing, severe stomach pain, muscle weakness or yellowing of skin/eyes
Do not breastfeed; tell your doctor if you are or may become pregnant
Zidovudine controls HIV but does not cure it and does not prevent passing HIV to others
pk: Rapid oral absorption; antiviral effect within hours intracellularly
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light
pearls: Boxed warning: hematologic toxicity (severe anemia and neutropenia), symptomatic myopathy with prolonged use, and lactic acidosis/severe hepatomegaly with steatosis
Historic and ongoing role in preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission (antepartum oral, intrapartum IV, neonatal prophylaxis)
Do NOT combine with stavudine or ribavirin (antagonism/toxicity); avoid other marrow-suppressive drugs where possible
Macrocytosis (raised MCV) is an expected effect and can serve as a rough adherence marker
Reduce dose in severe renal impairment; the glucuronide metabolite accumulates and is cleared by dialysis
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and continue your regular schedule. Do not double the dose. Consistent timing is important to maintain viral suppression.
overdose: Acute overdose (exposures up to ~50 g reported) has caused fatigue, headache, vomiting and occasional hematologic disturbances, with recovery and no permanent sequelae; seizures and CNS effects can occur. There is no specific antidote. Treatment is supportive with monitoring; hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis remove zidovudine negligibly but enhance elimination of the GZDV metabolite.
